sections.title: First Cycle of Dialogues
sections.description: Job and his friends debate the meaning of suffering

sections.title: Second Cycle of Dialogues
sections.description: His friends intensify their accusations against Job

sections.title: Third Cycle of Dialogues
sections.description: The final debate and the hymn to wisdom

sections.title: Job's Defense Speech
sections.description: Job looks back on his life and declares his innocence

sections.title: Elihu Speaks
sections.description: The young Elihu rebukes Job and his friends

sections.title: God Speaks
sections.description: God answers Job from the storm

events.title: Job's Righteousness and Prosperity
events.description: Job is described as a righteous and honest man who fears God and turns away from evil. He is the richest man in the East, with seven sons, three daughters, and enormous flocks of livestock. He regularly offers burnt offerings for his children in case they have sinned.

events.title: Satan's First Challenge
events.description: Satan comes before the Lord and claims that Job only fears God because he is blessed. God allows Satan to strike everything Job owns, but not to harm him personally. In a single day, Job loses all his oxen, donkeys, sheep, camels, and servants, and finally all ten of his children die when a house collapses on them. Job tears his robe and shaves his head, then falls down and worships: "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; may the name of the Lord be praised."

events.title: Satan's Second Challenge
events.description: Satan returns before the Lord and insists that Job will curse God if his own body is struck. God permits Satan to afflict Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Job's wife urges him to curse God and die, but Job rejects this, saying that we must accept both good and trouble from God.

events.title: Three Friends Arrive
events.description: Job's three friends Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite hear about his disaster and come to comfort him. They barely recognize him and sit with him for seven days and seven nights without speaking a word, because they see that his suffering is overwhelming.

events.title: Job Curses the Day He Was Born
events.description: Job breaks his silence and curses the day he was born. He wishes that day had never existed and asks why he did not die at birth. He longs for the rest of death and questions why God gives light to those who suffer and whose way is hidden.

events.title: Eliphaz's First Speech
events.description: Eliphaz argues that no innocent person has ever perished, and that suffering is a consequence of sin. He recounts a night vision in which a voice said that no one is righteous before God. He urges Job to turn back to God, for though God wounds, he also heals.

events.title: Job's Reply to Eliphaz
events.description: Job defends his complaint and says that his suffering is heavier than the sand of the sea. He accuses his friends of being unreliable like dried-up streams and asks God to tell him what he has done wrong. He describes the brevity and meaninglessness of life under his pain.

events.title: Bildad's First Speech and Job's Reply
events.description: Bildad claims that God never perverts justice and suggests that Job's children received their punishment. He urges Job to seek God. Job replies that he knows this, but asks how a human can be right before God. He longs for an intermediary who can lay a hand on both of them.

events.title: Zophar's First Speech and Job's Reply
events.description: Zophar accuses Job of empty talk and says that even some of his guilt is forgotten by God. He urges Job to set his heart right toward God. Job replies sarcastically that wisdom surely dies with them, and claims he does not fall short of them in insight. He challenges his friends and wants to present his case before God.

events.title: Second Cycle of Dialogues
events.description: Eliphaz sharpens the accusations and claims that Job undermines reverence for God with his words. Bildad describes the fate of the wicked. Zophar paints a picture of the brief triumph of the wicked. Job replies to them all, pointing out that the wicked often live in prosperity and peace, which contradicts his friends' simple theology of retribution.

events.title: Job's Profession of Faith: My Redeemer Lives
events.description: In the midst of his deepest despair, Job expresses a strong profession of faith: "I know that my Redeemer lives, and as the last he will stand upon the earth." He expresses hope that with his own eyes he will see God, even after his body has been consumed.

events.title: Third Cycle of Dialogues
events.description: Eliphaz now brings direct accusations of specific sins Job is said to have committed. Bildad speaks briefly about human insignificance before God. Job maintains his innocence and describes how he would defend himself before God. He reflects on the fate of the wicked and God's sovereign power.

events.title: The Hymn to Wisdom
events.description: Job sings a hymn to wisdom. Humans can mine precious stones from the depths of the earth and tame nature, but wisdom cannot be bought with gold nor found anywhere on earth. Only God knows the way to it, and he says to humanity: "To fear the Lord is wisdom."

events.title: Job's Defense Speech and Declaration of Innocence
events.description: Job looks back on his former honor and prosperity when God watched over him. He contrasts this with his current humiliation. Finally, he makes a solemn oath in which he disclaims any sin—lying, lust, oppression of servants, stinginess, idolatry, and hypocrisy—and challenges God to answer.

events.title: Elihu Speaks
events.description: The young Elihu, who had waited to speak out of respect for the elders, becomes angry because Job justifies himself rather than God, and because his friends have found no answers. He argues that God speaks through suffering to warn humanity, that God is righteous and almighty, and that God's greatness is incomprehensible, visible in nature's mighty forces.

events.title: God's First Speech from the Storm
events.description: The Lord answers Job out of the storm and asks him a series of rhetorical questions: Where were you when I laid the earth's foundation? Who marked off the boundaries of the sea? Can you command the morning star? God points to the wonders of creation—wildlife, weather phenomena, and natural laws—to reveal His incomprehensible wisdom and power.

events.title: God's Second Speech: Behemoth and Leviathan
events.description: God challenges Job again and describes two mighty creatures: Behemoth, with its immense strength and tail like a cedar, and Leviathan, the terrifying sea monster that no one can tame. Through these, God demonstrates that His power and sovereignty extend far beyond human understanding.

events.title: Job's Repentance
events.description: Job answers God and acknowledges that he has spoken of things he did not understand. He says: "I had only heard about you before, but now my eye has seen you." He repents in dust and ashes and humbly bows before God's sovereignty.

events.title: Job's Restoration
events.description: God rebukes Eliphaz and the other two friends for not speaking rightly about Him as Job did, and commands them to offer burnt offerings while Job prays for them. Then the Lord restores Job's fortunes and gives him twice as much as he had before. He is given seven sons and three daughters, and lives another 140 years.
